questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require immediate action.

rationale.correct: In neuromuscular weakness, vital capacity, inspiratory force and swallowing show danger long before SpO2 falls.

perOption.r1: Approaching the level where ventilation is needed.
perOption.r2: Weaker than -20 to -25 signals respiratory muscle failure.
perOption.r4: Rapid shallow breathing from weak muscles.
perOption.r5: Normal oxygen saturation is falsely reassuring; it falls late in neuromuscular failure.
perOption.r6: A typical sign of myasthenia, but not itself an emergency.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of impending respiratory failure in myasthenia gravis.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is more typical of myasthenic crisis or cholinergic crisis.

rows.text: Weakness that improved briefly after the dose, then worsened
Small pupils, sweating, drooling and abdominal cramps
Slow heart rate and wheezing
A new fluoroquinolone antibiotic
Muscle twitching (fasciculations) with weakness
Fever and infection

rationale.correct: Both cause weakness; muscarinic signs (SLUDGE, small pupils, bradycardia) point to cholinergic crisis.

perOption.r2:c1: Muscarinic excess from too much cholinesterase inhibitor.
perOption.r2:c2: Muscarinic excess from too much cholinesterase inhibitor.
perOption.r4:c1: Fluoroquinolones block neuromuscular transmission and trigger crisis.
perOption.r4:c2: Fluoroquinolones block neuromuscular transmission and trigger crisis.

questions.stem: For each order, indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated.

rows.text: Stop ciprofloxacin and choose another antibiotic
Plasmapheresis or IV immune globulin
Vital capacity and inspiratory force every 2 to 4 hours
Prepare for intubation if vital capacity falls below about 15 to 20 mL/kg
Another dose of pyridostigmine now to strengthen breathing
Magnesium sulfate for the urinary symptoms

rationale.correct: Remove the trigger, give immune therapy, watch the respiratory measures and secure the airway early.

perOption.r5:c1: Usually held in crisis while the client is ventilated or until the crisis type is clear; more can cause cholinergic crisis.
perOption.r5:c2: Usually held in crisis while the client is ventilated or until the crisis type is clear; more can cause cholinergic crisis.

exhibits.title: Plan, 1430
exhibits.body: ICU transfer. IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days. Stop ciprofloxacin; nitrofurantoin instead. Hold pyridostigmine if intubated. Neurology to see the client.

questions.stem: Review the 1700 findings. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Call the rapid response or anesthesia team for intubation
Suction the mouth and position the head up
Avoid sedatives and neuromuscular blockers unless the airway team directs them
Wait until the SpO2 falls below 90% before calling
Give a sip of water to test swallowing

rationale.correct: Act on vital capacity and secretions, not SpO2: protect the airway and call for intubation.

perOption.a: Vital capacity under 15 mL/kg with tiring.
perOption.b: Protects the airway from pooled secretions.
perOption.d: Clients with myasthenia are very sensitive to them.
perOption.e: SpO2 falls late; waiting risks arrest.

questions.stem: After recovery, the client describes the home plan. For each statement, indicate whether it shows understanding or needs more teaching.

rows.text: "I'll take pyridostigmine on time, about 30 to 60 minutes before meals."
"I'll check with my neurologist before taking any new antibiotic."
"If I'm weaker, I'll take extra doses until I feel better."
"I'll wear a medical alert bracelet."
"Drooling, sweating and cramps after a dose mean I should call."
"I'll rest in hot baths to relax my muscles."

rationale.correct: Safe self-care means timed doses, avoiding trigger drugs, not taking extra doses, and recognizing both crises.

perOption.r1:c1: Strength peaks for chewing and swallowing.
perOption.r1:c2: Strength peaks for chewing and swallowing.
perOption.r3:c1: Extra doses can cause cholinergic crisis; call instead.
perOption.r3:c2: Extra doses can cause cholinergic crisis; call instead.

questions.stem: On day 3, the client is intubated. The client blinks to answer questions and is clearly frightened. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Explain every procedure before doing it
Set up a reliable way to communicate, such as a blink code or letter board

questions.stem: Complete the sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

content.template: Right-sided weakness is explained by {{b1}}. The headache and vomiting suggest {{b2}}. Alteplase is {{b3}}.

options.text: a left-sided brain lesion, because motor pathways cross

rationale.correct: A left basal ganglia bleed causes right weakness; ICP is rising; thrombolysis is contraindicated.

perOption.b1:a: The left hemisphere controls the right body.
perOption.b3:a: Thrombolysis is never given for a hemorrhagic stroke.
perOption.b3:b: Only for ischemic stroke without bleeding.

questions.stem: Six weeks later, on the rehabilitation unit, review the findings. Which actions should the nurse take first? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sit the client upright with the legs down
Loosen tight clothing and the leg bag straps
Check the urinary catheter for kinks and the bladder for distension
Check blood pressure every 2 to 5 minutes
Lay the client flat and raise the legs
Wait for the provider before doing anything

rationale.correct: Autonomic dysreflexia: sit up, loosen clothing, find and remove the trigger (bladder, bowel, skin), monitor BP.

perOption.a: Lowers blood pressure by pooling blood.
perOption.c: The bladder is the most common trigger.
perOption.f: Autonomic dysreflexia is an emergency the nurse acts on at once.

questions.stem: Before discharge, the client and partner describe how to prevent and treat autonomic dysreflexia. For each statement, indicate whether it shows understanding or needs more teaching.

rows.text: "We'll keep a schedule for bladder and bowel care."
"If a headache starts, I'll sit up and check my catheter first."
"We'll carry the emergency card that explains dysreflexia."
"A blood pressure of 150/90 is normal for me."
"I'll lie down flat if I feel a headache."
"We'll check my skin twice a day for pressure areas."

rationale.correct: Prevention routines, the first steps, the emergency card and knowing the baseline BP.

perOption.r3:c1: Helps clinicians who may not recognize it.
perOption.r3:c2: Helps clinicians who may not recognize it.
perOption.r4:c1: Their baseline is about 96/60; 150/90 may be dysreflexia.
perOption.r4:c2: Their baseline is about 96/60; 150/90 may be dysreflexia.
perOption.r6:c1: Skin injury is a trigger and a risk.

exhibits.title: Neurology unit, 1400
exhibits.body: A 46-year-old client with myasthenia gravis takes pyridostigmine 60 mg four times daily. A week ago the client started ciprofloxacin for a urinary infection. Today the client has drooping eyelids, double vision, slurred and nasal speech, and trouble swallowing saliva. The client cannot lift the arms for long and says breathing feels weak. The client took two extra pyridostigmine tablets this morning "to help."

exhibits.title: Medical unit, admission
exhibits.body: A 38-year-old client had a diarrheal illness 3 weeks ago. Over 4 days, tingling began in the feet and weakness has climbed to the thighs and now the hands. Knee and ankle reflexes are absent. The client is alert and anxious. Lumbar puncture: high protein with a normal cell count.

exhibits.title: Emergency department, 0915
exhibits.body: A 74-year-old client who takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation had a sudden severe headache at 0830, then vomiting and right-sided weakness. The client is drowsy. CT: a 30 mL left basal ganglia hemorrhage.
